title: Squares of a Sorted Array
summary: You get a list of integers `nums`, sorted from smallest to largest; some of them may be negative. Return a new list holding the square of every number, also sorted from smallest to largest. Squaring everything and then sorting works, but aim for O(n) time.

examples.explanation: In input order the squares are [36, 4, 0, 9, 25]: largest at the two ends, smallest in the middle.
When every number is negative, squaring reverses the order.

constraints: nums is sorted from smallest to largest; equal values may repeat

approaches.twist: Fill the result from the back with the larger square of the two ends, then move that pointer inward.
Square every number, then sort the squares.
approaches.note: Works, but sorting the squares takes O(n log n) time. nums is already sorted, so the target is O(n).

signals.meaning: Sorted order puts the biggest squares at the two ends: the most negative number or the largest positive one. Compare the two ends instead of sorting again.
Squaring flips the order of negatives: −7 is smaller than 5, but its square, 49, is larger than 25. So the squares are large at both ends and small in the middle.
Sorting the squares costs O(n log n). The input is already sorted, so one pass from both ends can place every square in order.

constraintReading: len(nums) is at most 10⁴, so squaring and sorting, O(n log n), would run fast: the size alone allows it. The O(n) time target is what rules out the sort. The answer list itself takes O(n) space; beyond it, two indexes and a write position are enough.

related.relation: Same pointers at the two ends of a sorted list, but a sum compared with a target decides which one moves instead of the larger square.
